description.content: A Workspace arranges tabsets that users can rearrange by dragging tabs: between tabsets, within a tabset's list of tabs, or onto the edge of a tabset to split it. Tabsets can be resized and maximized.

The layout is described by a serializable model (see WorkspaceModel). Workspaces are uncontrolled: provide an initial model with the defaultModel prop, save changes from the onModelChanged callback, and make changes using the imperative API (see WorkspaceImperativeHandle).
Tab content is not remounted when a tab is moved. Its elements are moved within the document, though, which resets some browser state (e.g. iframes are reloaded).
Workspace elements always include the following attributes:
<div data-workspace data-testid="workspace-id-prop" id="workspace-id-prop">
Test id can be used to narrow selection when unit testing.
CSS class name.
Uniquely identifies this workspace within an application. Falls back to useId when not provided.
This value will also be assigned to the id and data-testid attributes (an explicit data-testid prop will take precedence).

id.html: id?: string | number
id.name: id

description.content: CSS properties.

Lets the workspace accept drags that use the browser's drag and drop from outside of any workspace (e.g. an element of the application with the draggable attribute, a file, or a link from another application), showing the drop indicator while the drag is over the workspace, and creating a tab where it's dropped. The new tab is reported to onModelChanged with the "add" reason.

disableDrop can't be called until the tab is created (when the drag is dropped), so a target it rejects is shown as accepted while dragging; the drop is ignored then. Drag sources within the application can use the imperative startExternalDrag method instead, which doesn't have this limitation.
Elements within the workspace's tab content that handle the same drags themselves (by canceling the dragover and drop events) take precedence.
This object is read when drag events are handled, so it doesn't need to be memoized.

description.content:
CSS class names for the elements the workspace renders within its root element:

  • tabset: root element of a tabset (data-tabset)
  • header: contains a tabset's tab list and toolbar (data-tabset-header)
  • tabList: contains a tabset's tabs (data-tab-list)
  • tab: passed to renderTab with the rest of a tab's props (data-tab)
  • toolbar: contains the content returned by renderTabsetToolbar (data-tabset-toolbar)
  • tabPanels: contains a tabset's tab content (data-tab-panels)
  • tabContent: the element each tab's content is rendered into (data-tab-content)
  • dropIndicator: shows where a dragged tab will be dropped within a tabset's panels, or at an edge of the workspace (data-drop-indicator)
  • dragPreview: follows the pointer while a tab or tabset is dragged (data-drag-preview)

Elements expose their state as data attributes (e.g. data-tab-selected, or data-tabset-dragging while a tabset is dragged), which can be used for styling. Elements within a collapsed tabset have a data-tabset-collapsed attribute. Elements within a tabset also have a data-tab-placement attribute (see tabPlacement).

The drop indicator is the same element for the whole drag (rendered within the workspace's root element), so it can be animated between regions and tabsets (e.g. transition: inset 250ms). Its data-region attribute is the region of a tabset's panels it covers, or its data-edge attribute is the edge of the workspace it's at; while a tab isn't over either, it has neither and isn't shown (opacity: 0).
Like the render props, this object is part of what tabsets re-render for; in large workspaces, define it outside of the component (or memoize it) rather than inline.
Initial layout of the workspace.
Splits and tabsets may omit their ids; they're assigned ids based on their position (see WorkspaceModelInput).
This value is only used when the Workspace mounts; use the imperative setModel method to replace it later.

description.content: Lets tabs be copied by dragging them: a tab dropped while the copy modifier key is held (Option on macOS, Ctrl elsewhere) adds the copy this function returns, leaving the dragged tab where it was. The change is reported to onModelChanged with the "copy" reason.

Returning null (or undefined) moves the dragged tab instead. If that move isn't allowed either (the disableDrop prop rejects it, the ids conflict, or it isn't a valid place to move the tab), nothing happens.
The copy needs an id that isn't used by any other node of the workspace (e.g. crypto.randomUUID()); copies with ids that are in use are rejected (and the tab is moved instead).

The workspace the tab is dropped into makes the copy, so a tab dragged from another workspace (see the dragGroup prop) is copied by the workspace it's dropped into (and is only copied if that workspace has this prop).

  • tab The tab being dragged
  • target Where the copy will be dropped

copyTab.html: copyTab?: ((tab: TabNode<TabData>, target: TabDropTarget) => TabNode<TabData> | null) | undefined
copyTab.name: copyTab

description.content: Lets tabsets be copied by dragging them (by their headers), like the copyTab prop does for tabs: a tabset dropped while the copy modifier key is held adds the copy this function returns, leaving the dragged tabset where it was. The change is reported to onModelChanged with the "copy" reason.
The copy includes its tabs, which need ids that aren't used by any other node of the workspace too; the copyTab argument copies a tab:
copyTabset={(tabset, copyTab) => ({ ...tabset, id: crypto.randomUUID(), tabs: tabset.tabs.map(copyTab) })}

Returning null (or undefined) moves the dragged tabset instead. If that move isn't allowed either (the disableDrop prop rejects it, the ids conflict, a keepWhenEmpty tabset is dropped into another workspace, or it isn't a valid place to move the tabset), nothing happens.
The copy's selected tab is the copy of the dragged tabset's selected tab (matched by position), unless the copy selects one of its own tabs.

A copy dropped into a tab list (or onto the center of another tabset) only adds its tabs; its id and data are only used where it's added as a tabset.

  • tabset The tabset being dragged
  • copyTab Copies a tab with the copyTab prop (and the same drop target); without that prop (or if it returns null), the copy is a shallow copy of the tab with a new id
  • target Where the copy will be dropped

copyTabset.name: copyTabset

description.content: Locks the arrangement: tabs cannot be resized, dragged, dropped, or closed by the user. Selecting tabs and maximizing tabsets still work.
This prop overrides the disableClose and disableDrag flags of individual tabs.

Keeps drags between workspaces (see dragGroup) within this copy of the application: tabs dragged from this workspace can't be dropped into other copies of the application (e.g. the application loaded in another browser window or tab), and tabs dragged from other copies can't be dropped into this workspace. Workspaces in popout windows rendered by this copy of the application (with portals) are still part of the group.
Defaults to false, so that workspaces with the same dragGroup in other copies of the application from the same origin can exchange tabs.
Prevents tabs (and tabsets) from being dropped onto some (or all) targets.
Functions are called when the target under the pointer changes; returning true rejects the target.
While a tabset is dragged, this function is called for each of its tabs (see DisableDropArgs), so restrictions on where tabs can be dropped apply to dragged tabsets too.

Tabs can also be dropped at the edges of the workspace (beside all of the other tabsets), within a few pixels of the edges of its layout (except over tabset headers, where the tab lists are) or within its root element's padding. These targets have an edge rather than a tabsetId; disableDrop={({ target }) => "edge" in target} turns them off.

disableDrop.html: disableDrop?: boolean | ((args: DisableDropArgs<TabData, TabsetData>) => boolean)
disableDrop.name: disableDrop

description.content: Lets tabs (and tabsets) be dragged between workspaces with the same dragGroup, including workspaces in popout windows (opened by the application and rendered into with a portal) and in other copies of the application from the same origin, e.g. the application loaded in another browser window or tab (see disableDragBetweenApps). Dropping one into another workspace moves it there, keeping its id and data; both workspaces report the change to onModelChanged with the "transfer" reason.

Mouse drags use the browser's drag and drop when this prop is set, since pointer events can't follow the pointer into another window. Touch drags still use pointer events, so they can't leave the window.

Tab ids must be unique within the group; a tab can't be dropped into a workspace that already has a tab with its id (and a tabset with the keepWhenEmpty flag can't be dragged to another workspace). A tab dragged to another workspace is rendered by that workspace, so its content is mounted again.

A tab dragged to another copy of the application is sent there with the structured clone algorithm (like postMessage), so its data must be cloneable (e.g. no functions); tabs whose data can't be cloned (and tabsets containing them) can only be dragged within their copy of the application. Copies loaded at different times may be running different versions of the application, so the other copy may need to handle tab data it doesn't recognize.
Ref attached to the root HTMLDivElement.

elementRef.name: elementRef

description.content: What happens to the content of tabs that are not selected. Can be a function to choose per tab (e.g. based on its data).

• "keep-mounted": content stays mounted (and its effects keep running)
  • "activity": content stays mounted but is rendered within a hidden React <Activity> boundary, so its effects are unmounted; requires React 19.2 (falls back to "keep-mounted" otherwise)
  • "unmount": content is unmounted
Moving a tab never remounts its content.
Its React state is preserved, but its elements are moved within the document, which resets some browser state: iframes are reloaded, playing media is paused, and focused elements are blurred.

hiddenTabBehavior.html: hiddenTabBehavior?: HiddenTabBehavior | ((tab: TabNode<TabData>) => HiddenTabBehavior) = "keep-mounted"
hiddenTabBehavior.name: hiddenTabBehavior

description.content: Called after the model has changed (e.g. a tab was moved, selected, or closed, or a tabset was resized).
For changes caused by pointer events, this callback is not called until the pointer has been released. This callback is recommended for saving models to storage.

onModelChanged.html: onModelChanged?: (model: WorkspaceModel<TabData, TabsetData>, meta: WorkspaceChangedMeta) => void
onModelChanged.name: onModelChanged

description.content: Called when a tab (or a whole tabset) is dropped outside of the window, e.g. to open it in a popup window. Return true to accept it, which removes it from this workspace (reported to onModelChanged with the "tear-off" reason); otherwise nothing changes.
Tabs and tabsets can only be torn off if they could be dragged, and tabsets with the keepWhenEmpty flag can't be torn off. Without this prop, dropping a tab outside of the window does nothing.

The Workspace can't tell whether the application showed the tab, so check whether window.open returned null (because the popup was blocked) and return false then to keep the tab; returning true removes it even if nothing shows it.

This is called while the release of the pointer is being handled (which browsers treat as user input), so a popup can be opened from it. With the dragGroup prop, a tab is torn off when it's dropped outside of every window in the group; the end of those drags isn't treated as user input, so browsers block popups opened then unless the drag started a few seconds earlier at most (and Safari blocks them always).

Deprecated: browsers don't reliably report where a drag that leaves the window ends, and some block popups opened at the end of a drag. Open popout windows from a button instead (see usePopoutWindows). This will be removed in the next major version.
This prop has been deprecated. Open popout windows from a button instead (see usePopoutWindows).

onTearOff.name: onTearOff

description.content: Content of the element that follows the pointer while a tab is being dragged. Defaults to the tab's title (or id).
The element has a data-tear-off attribute while releasing the pointer would tear off the tab (see the deprecated onTearOff prop).

renderDragPreview.name: renderDragPreview

description.content: Content of the element that follows the pointer while a whole tabset is being dragged. Defaults to the title (or id) of its selected tab followed by the number of other tabs being dragged (e.g. "One (+2)"), or the selected tab's renderDragPreview when that prop is set, or the tabset's id if it has no tabs.

The element has a data-drag-type attribute: "tabset" while a tabset is dragged, and "tab" while a tab is. It also has a data-tear-off attribute while releasing the pointer would tear off the tabset (see the deprecated onTearOff prop).

description.content: Separator rendered between the children of a split. Should return a Separator (or null for no separator); defaults to an unstyled Separator.

Without separators, tabsets can still be resized by dragging their edges (like Panels in a Group without separators), but separators are recommended: they can be resized with the keyboard, and an edge's hit area can overlap the tabs beside it (pressing there resizes the tabset rather than dragging the tab).

renderSeparator.name: renderSeparator

description.content: Renders a tab (within its tabset's tab list). Spread props onto the returned element: they make it a tab (its role and ARIA attributes, keyboard and pointer handling, and data attributes), and attach a ref that dragging and keyboard focus depend on.

renderTab={(tab, props) => (
<div {...props}>
{tab.title}
<TabCloseButton />
</div>
)}
Individual props can be overridden or wrapped, e.g. to confirm before the Delete key closes a tab (call props.onKeyDown for other keys).

Merge className and style rather than replacing them (e.g. style={{ ...props.style, padding: 4 }}): they include the tab entries of the classNames and styles props, and style includes the touch-action that touch dragging depends on.

Pointer events from interactive descendants (button elements, form controls such as input (and the label elements of form controls), editable content, elements with a button or form control role such as role="checkbox", or elements with a data-tab-ignore attribute) are ignored, so clicking a button within a tab doesn't select or drag it, and pressing within an input (e.g. one used to rename the tab) doesn't start a drag. Keys pressed within any descendant (rather than the tab itself) are left to it, so they don't move focus between tabs or close the tab.
When this prop is not provided, tabs show their title (or id) followed by a TabCloseButton.

renderTab.name: renderTab

Content is only re-rendered when its tab changes or this function does; a function created while rendering (e.g. an inline arrow function) re-renders the content of every tab whenever the Workspace's parent re-renders, so it should be memoized (e.g. with useCallback) when tab content is expensive to render.

description.content: Render the content of selected tabs on the server. Can be a function to choose per tab (e.g. based on its data).

Tab content is rendered through portals (so that moving a tab doesn't remount it), which React can't render on the server. Content opted into server rendering is rendered inline instead, then moved into a portal once hydration has finished.

That move remounts the content once (e.g. resetting its state and re-running its effects), so this is best suited to content that is cheap to mount and benefits from being in the server-rendered HTML.
This prop has no effect for workspaces that are not server rendered.

serverRenderTabContent.name: serverRenderTabContent

description.content: CSS properties for the elements the workspace renders within its root element (see classNames).
Where tabs are placed relative to tab content.
Tabs placed on the left or right are stacked ("vertical"): this determines how a dropped tab's position is found and which arrow keys move focus between tabs.
Elements within a tabset have a data-tab-placement attribute, which can be used for styling (e.g. rotating tabs on the left or right).

"left" and "right" are the start and end of the tabset (its header is rendered before or after its content), so in a right-to-left layout (e.g. within dir="rtl") tabs placed on the "left" are on the right; styles for them should use logical properties (e.g. border-inline-end rather than border-right).
Tabsets can override this with the tabPlacement field of their model node.

tabPlacement.html: tabPlacement?: "bottom" | "left" | "right" | "top" = "top"
tabPlacement.name: tabPlacement

description.content:
Which tab is selected when a tabset's selected tab is removed (closed, or dragged to another tabset):

  • "adjacent": the tab after it (or before it, if it was the last tab)
  • "recent": the tabset's most recently selected tab (like an IDE's editor groups), falling back to "adjacent" if none of its other tabs has been selected
In "recent" mode, each tabset's recently selected tabs are saved in the model (see TabsetNode.recentTabIds), so they're restored with the rest of the layout.

tabRemovalSelectionBehavior.name: tabRemovalSelectionBehavior

description.content: Minimum height of each tabset's content area (not including its header).
Tabsets can override this with the minHeight field of their model node.

Interpretation rules:

  • Strings must specify a unit: "px", "em", "rem", "vh", or "vw" (e.g. tabsetMinHeight: "200px")
  • Percentages (and strings without units) are not allowed
